rows.prompt: Who will be the prime minister of Japan in 2040?
rows.answer:
Unknown. 🇯🇵

Japan’s Prime Minister serves at the pleasure of the Diet (parliament) and has no constitutional term limits. The office rotates based on party leadership contests and general elections, which must be held at least every four years.

Because political landscapes shift rapidly, it is impossible to name a specific individual today who will hold the seat in 2040. It will simply be whoever wins the ruling party’s leadership race or the general election closest to that date.

It’s essentially a game of musical chairs where the music never quite stops playing for long. The Prime Minister isn’t elected directly by the people in a general election; instead, they are chosen from among members of the Diet (Japan’s parliament). Specifically, whoever leads the party that holds the majority in the House of Representatives becomes PM. Since there is no constitutional term limit on how many times someone can be re-elected or re-appointed as leader, it is theoretically possible for one person to hold the office indefinitely—as long as they keep winning their seat and retaining the support of their party’s lawmakers.

To see why this makes 2040 so hard to predict, look at Shinzo Abe. He served two non-consecutive terms totaling nearly eight years (from 2012 to 2020), making him one of the longest-serving leaders in modern Japanese history. If political conditions were favorable—say, a stable economy and strong party unity—a current leader like Shigeru Ishiba or even Fumio Kishida could potentially ride their popularity through multiple leadership contests over the next fifteen years. Conversely, if scandals hit (which they often do in LDP politics) or public sentiment shifts sharply toward smaller parties, the seat could change hands every year or two until 2040 arrives with a completely new face at the helm.

So while we know how the person will be chosen—a vote by their peers followed by parliamentary confirmation—we don’t yet know who that peer group will favor in fifteen years’ time. It depends entirely on which party holds power then, and whether any single politician can maintain enough internal support to stay at the top for another decade or more.
